verifyNote: Written from standard UK binocular vision practice. Always check against Dr Sheppard's slides — criteria and normal values vary between textbooks and clinics.

topics.title: Heterophoria and heterotropia
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: a phoria is a latent deviation held by fusion; a tropia is manifest with both eyes open. The cover test is the only objective test that tells them apart, and the real question with a phoria is whether it's compensated.
keyPoints: Covering one eye dissociates the eyes: fusion stops, so the covered eye moves to its passive position, revealing any phoria.
Tropia on cover/uncover of the other eye: the deviated eye moves to fixate: out for esotropia, in for exotropia, down for hypertropia, up for hypotropia.
Phoria on uncovering: out = esophoria, in = exophoria, down = hyper on that side, up = hypo; phorias are usually similar in size in each eye. Smooth fast recovery suggests compensation.
The alternating cover test reveals the total deviation (as when tired or stressed) and any intermittent tropia; cover/uncover shows the habitual one.
Decompensated phoria can give fixation disparity, measured with the Mallett unit.
Prescription changes affect phorias: more minus can decompensate esophoria, more plus exophoria.
examTraps: Mixing up the direction: the eye moving outwards to take up fixation means it was turned in (eso).
Treating any phoria as abnormal: what matters is compensation and symptoms.

diagram.description: Pairs of eyes viewing a target. Top row (phoria): both eyes straight when uncovered; under a cover the covered eye drifts out (exophoria). Bottom row (tropia): with both eyes open the left eye is turned out (exotropia).
labels: Phoria: straight with both eyes open
Tropia: deviation with both eyes open

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: compensation criteria
goDeeper.body: Sheard's criterion (fusional reserve opposing the phoria should be at least twice the phoria) and Percival's criterion are common ways to judge compensation alongside symptoms and fixation disparity. Decompensated phoria typically causes eyestrain, headaches, blur and intermittent diplopia with sustained tasks.

flashcards.back: Phoria = latent (fusion holds it); tropia = manifest with both eyes open.
A small exophoria at near is normal.

mcq.q: Near exophoria 6Δ, base-out reserve to blur 15Δ. Does it meet Sheard's criterion?

options.text: No — the reserve must be 3 × the phoria
options.feedback: Sheard uses twice, not three times.

options.text: No — you need the base-in reserve
options.feedback: For exophoria, the opposing reserve is base-out (convergent).
Sheard can be applied on its own.

mcq.explanation: Sheard: compensating (opposing) reserve ≥ 2 × phoria. For exo, the compensating reserve is convergent (base-out).

mcq.q: Near exophoria 12Δ, base-out reserve to blur 12Δ. Sheard prism?

options.feedback: Exophoria is relieved with base-in prism.
Subtract a third of the reserve.
12Δ is less than 2 × 12Δ, so it fails Sheard.

mcq.explanation: Sheard prism = 2/3 phoria − 1/3 reserve; base direction is base in for exo.

mcq.q: What is a heterophoria?

options.text: A latent deviation held straight by fusion
A manifest deviation with both eyes open
A refractive error held in by accommodation
A field defect found only on cover

mcq.explanation: A heterophoria is a tendency for the eyes to deviate that is kept in check by fusion, so it only shows when fusion is broken, for example by covering.

mcq.q: On uncovering, the eye moves outwards. What phoria is this?
mcq.explanation: Under the cover the eye drifted inwards (esophoria), so on uncovering it moves outwards to regain fixation.

mcq.q: Which is normal at near?
mcq.explanation: A small exophoria at near is normal because the eyes don't fully converge for the target when dissociated.

mcq.q: A student has a 6Δ exophoria at near. Which symptom would most suggest it's decompensating?

options.text: Words doubling and eyestrain when studying
Flashes of light in the periphery
Itchy, watery eyes in the evening
Blur at distance that clears at near

mcq.explanation: Decompensated phorias cause intermittent diplopia, eyestrain and headaches with sustained tasks.

original.q: Which symptom suggests decompensated phoria?

options.text: Intermittent diplopia and eyestrain with sustained tasks

mcq.q: More plus for a young exophore can
mcq.explanation: More plus reduces accommodation, and with it accommodative convergence, so an exophoria can increase and decompensate.

mcq.q: On the alternating cover test, the right eye recovers from 4Δ exo. What do you expect from the left eye?

options.feedback: Yes: a phoria is usually similar in each eye.

mcq.explanation: Phorias measured in each eye are usually similar in size.

original.q: Phorias in each eye are usually

options.feedback: Most people have a small one.

mcq.q: Cover/uncover shows no tropia, but the alternating cover test leaves the left eye drifting out until the patient blinks. What does that reveal?

options.text: A constant tropia of the left eye

mcq.explanation: The alternating cover test reveals the total deviation and any intermittent tropia.

original.q: Which test reveals intermittent tropia?

mcq.q: Two patients each have 8Δ exophoria at near. One has symptoms and poor recovery; the other doesn't. What's the key difference?
mcq.explanation: What matters most about a phoria is whether it's compensated.

original.q: What matters most about a phoria?

mcq.q: On uncovering, the eye moves inwards. What phoria is this?
mcq.explanation: Under the cover the eye drifted outwards (exophoria), so on uncovering it moves inwards to regain fixation.

mcq.q: What's a normal distance phoria?
mcq.explanation: At distance, most people are orthophoric or have a small exophoria.

mcq.q: Near esophoria 6Δ, base-in reserve to blur 6Δ. Sheard prism?
mcq.explanation: Sheard's prism = (2/3 × phoria) − (1/3 × opposing reserve) = 4 − 2 = 2Δ; esophoria is relieved with base-out prism.

mcq.q: Which reserve does Sheard use for an esophoria?

options.text: None: Sheard is for exo only

mcq.explanation: Sheard compares the phoria with the opposing fusional reserve. For esophoria that's the base-in (divergent) reserve.

mcq.q: Percival's criterion says

options.text: the patient should work in the middle third of their range
the opposing reserve should be twice the phoria
the phoria should measure zero at near
acuity must be 6/6 in each eye

mcq.explanation: Percival's criterion says the patient should be working in the middle third of their total vergence range.

mcq.q: With +1.00 D, a near phoria changes from 2Δ exo to 6Δ exo. Gradient AC/A?
mcq.explanation: Gradient AC/A = change in phoria ÷ change in lens power = 4Δ (from 2 to 6 exo) ÷ 1.00 D = 4Δ/D.

mcq.q: PD 6 cm, distance ortho, near 3Δ exo at 40 cm. Calculated AC/A?
mcq.explanation: Calculated AC/A = PD (cm) + (near phoria − distance phoria) ÷ near demand = 6 + (−3 − 0) ÷ 2.5 = 4.8Δ/D, with exo taken as negative.

mcq.q: Esophoria much larger at near than distance with a high AC/A suggests
mcq.explanation: More eso at near than distance with a high AC/A means too much convergence at near: convergence excess, which a near add can help.

mcq.q: Exodeviation larger at distance than near suggests
mcq.explanation: An exodeviation that's larger at distance than near is the pattern of divergence excess.

mcq.q: A phoria is compensated when

options.text: there are no symptoms and recovery is good
it's large enough to measure easily

mcq.explanation: A phoria is compensated when it causes no symptoms and the eyes recover quickly and smoothly after cover.

mcq.q: What is orthophoria?

options.text: No deviation when fusion is broken
A latent deviation held by fusion
A manifest deviation with eyes open
Double vision when one eye is covered

mcq.explanation: Orthophoria means no deviation at all when fusion is broken: the eyes stay perfectly aligned.

mcq.q: A heterotropia is

options.text: a manifest deviation with both eyes open
a latent deviation held by fusion
normal in most adults at near
found only when looking at near

mcq.explanation: A heterotropia (squint) is a manifest deviation, present even with both eyes open.

mcq.q: Which are Maddox's components of vergence?
mcq.explanation: Maddox described four components of vergence: tonic, accommodative, fusional and proximal.

mcq.q: Exophoria 8Δ, base-out reserve to blur 10Δ. Sheard prism?
mcq.explanation: Sheard's prism = (2/3 × 8) − (1/3 × 10) ≈ 5.3 − 3.3 = 2Δ; exophoria is relieved with base-in prism.

mcq.q: Exophoria 4Δ, base-out reserve to blur 12Δ. Sheard prism?

options.feedback: Yes: the reserve is at least twice the phoria.

mcq.explanation: Sheard is met when the opposing reserve is at least twice the phoria: 12Δ is more than 2 × 4Δ, so no prism is needed.

mcq.q: Which instrument measures the near phoria at 33 cm?
mcq.explanation: The Maddox wing measures the near phoria at 33 cm, using an arrow seen by one eye and a scale seen by the other.

mcq.q: Looking through a horizontal Maddox rod, the patient sees

options.feedback: Yes: the streak is perpendicular to the rod axis.

mcq.explanation: A Maddox rod turns a spot of light into a streak at 90° to the cylinders, so horizontal cylinders give a vertical line.

mcq.q: A Maddox rod with its cylinders horizontal measures
mcq.explanation: With horizontal cylinders the patient sees a vertical line, which is used to measure horizontal phoria.

mcq.q: Which test measures cyclophoria?
mcq.explanation: The double Maddox rod gives two lines; their relative tilt shows cyclophoria.

mcq.q: A normal AC/A ratio is about
mcq.explanation: A normal AC/A ratio is about 4 ± 2Δ/D, so roughly 3–5Δ/D.

mcq.q: With −1.00 D, a near phoria changes from 2Δ exo to 2Δ eso. Gradient AC/A?
mcq.explanation: Gradient AC/A = phoria change ÷ lens change. 2Δ exo to 2Δ eso is a 4Δ change for 1.00 D, so 4Δ/D.

mcq.q: Esophoria larger at distance than near suggests
mcq.explanation: Esophoria that's larger at distance than near is the pattern of divergence insufficiency.

mcq.q: Exophoria equal at distance and near suggests
mcq.explanation: An exophoria that's similar at distance and near is called basic exophoria.

mcq.q: A common cause of esophoria in children is
mcq.explanation: Uncorrected hyperopia makes a child accommodate more, and the extra accommodative convergence causes esophoria.

mcq.q: Even a small vertical phoria can be symptomatic because
mcq.explanation: Vertical fusional reserves are only a few prism dioptres, so even a small vertical phoria can be hard to control.

mcq.q: Which factor can make a phoria decompensate?

options.text: Fatigue, illness or more near work

mcq.explanation: Fatigue, illness and more near work reduce the ability to control a phoria, so it can decompensate.

mcq.q: Which is a symptom of decompensated phoria?
mcq.explanation: When a phoria decompensates, fusion slips, giving intermittent diplopia or words moving on the page.

mcq.q: Morgan's norm for near base-out break is roughly
mcq.explanation: Morgan's expected value for the near base-out break is about 21Δ.

mcq.q: Morgan's norm for distance base-in break is roughly
mcq.explanation: Morgan's expected value for the distance base-in break is about 7Δ.

mcq.q: Fusional reserves are recorded as

options.text: a single number in prism dioptres

mcq.explanation: Fusional reserves are recorded as three points: blur, break and recovery.

mcq.q: Which treatment suits an esophoria from uncorrected hyperopia?
mcq.explanation: Correcting the hyperopia reduces accommodation and the accommodative convergence that causes the esophoria.

mcq.q: Which test uses a dot card or Howell card to measure phoria?
mcq.explanation: The Howell card measures the phoria using a numbered scale and a vertical prism to separate the images.

mcq.q: The von Graefe technique uses

options.text: vertical prism to dissociate, horizontal to measure
a red glass over one eye with a spotlight
a cover alone, moved from eye to eye
the polarised strips of a Mallett unit

mcq.explanation: In the von Graefe technique, vertical prism dissociates the eyes and horizontal prism is varied to measure the phoria.

mcq.q: An intermittent exotropia that breaks down when tired is often
mcq.explanation: Intermittent exotropia typically shows more at distance and tends to break down with tiredness.

mcq.q: Which option can help an exophore with symptoms?
mcq.explanation: Vergence exercises build up convergent reserves so a symptomatic exophore can control the deviation.

mcq.q: Prism for a symptomatic exophore is
mcq.explanation: Base-in prism moves the image outwards (towards the apex), matching where the exophoric eye tends to point.

mcq.q: Which records an exophoria that recovers well at near?
mcq.explanation: The record should give distance, type, size and quality of recovery, for example 'N: 6Δ XOP, good recovery'.

mcq.q: Fixation disparity is

options.text: a tiny misalignment within Panum's area
double vision that comes and goes

mcq.explanation: Fixation disparity is a tiny misalignment of the eyes that is still within Panum's area, so the patient sees single.

mcq.q: Surgery for a phoria is

options.text: rarely needed, for large symptomatic cases
never carried out for a phoria

mcq.explanation: Surgery is rarely needed for a phoria and is kept for large, symptomatic cases that don't respond to other treatment.

mcq.q: The ratio of accommodative convergence to accommodation is the
mcq.explanation: The AC/A ratio is the amount of accommodative convergence (in Δ) per dioptre of accommodation.

cases.scenario: On cover test at distance, neither eye moves when the other is covered. On the alternating cover test, each eye moves inwards as it is uncovered.
cases.question: What is the deviation and how do you decide whether it matters?
cases.modelAnswer: No movement on the cover-uncover test means there is no manifest deviation (no tropia). An inward recovery movement means the eye had drifted out under cover: an exophoria. Whether it matters depends on compensation: ask about symptoms such as headaches, eyestrain or intermittent diplopia, watch the speed and smoothness of recovery, measure the size, and check fusional reserves, fixation disparity (Mallett unit) and near point of convergence. A well-compensated, symptom-free phoria needs no treatment.

topics.askClaude: Give me phoria measurements with fusional reserves and ask me whether each meets Sheard's criterion and what prism (if any) it suggests.

topics.title: The cover test
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: the cover test is objective and the only test that distinguishes phoria from tropia. Do it in three stages at distance and near, first with the habitual and then the optimal correction.
keyPoints: Set-up: room lights on, a lamp can help you see the eyes, target one line larger than the worse eye's VA (spotlight if worse than about 6/18), primary gaze.
Stage 1, cover/uncover for tropia: cover the left, watch the right for 2–3 seconds; uncover and watch it return; then repeat the other way.
Stage 2, cover/uncover for phoria (only if no tropia): watch the covered eye as it's uncovered; it recovers to the active position.
Stage 3, alternating cover: move the cover quickly between eyes for 10–30 seconds to stop fusion and show the total deviation and any intermittent tropia.
Near: same steps with the near correction, a detailed target on a near stick; consider looking down if there are near symptoms.
Size: estimate (1 cm at 1 m = 1Δ) or neutralise with a prism bar during the alternating cover (base in for exo, base out for eso) to find the objective angle.
examTraps: Doing the alternating cover first: it can break down a phoria before you've checked for a tropia.
Using a light at distance when VA allows letters: you lose control of accommodation.
Getting the prism base direction backwards.

diagram.description: Sequence of four eye pairs: (1) both eyes fixating; (2) right eye covered — left eye stays still (no left tropia); (3) cover removed — right eye moves in from an outward position (exophoria recovery); (4) alternate cover between eyes showing each eye moving in as it's uncovered.

goDeeper.heading: Worked SAQ: right esotropia
goDeeper.body: Cover LE: RE moves out to fixate and LE moves in under the cover (Hering's law). Uncover LE: RE moves back in and LE moves out. Cover RE: no movement. Uncover RE: no movement.

goDeeper.heading: Versional recovery
goDeeper.body: Some patients with large phorias or marked dominance recover with a version (both eyes move) followed by a vergence, which obeys Hering's law, instead of only the covered eye moving.

checklist.title: Cover test routine
steps: Distance target: a letter one or two lines above the worse eye's VA.
Cover the right eye; watch the left for movement (tropia?).
Uncover the right eye; watch it for recovery (phoria direction, speed).
Alternate cover several times; note direction and estimate size.
Measure with a prism bar if needed.
Repeat at near with an accommodative target.
Record direction, size, recovery, distance and near (e.g. 'D: ortho; N: 6Δ XOP, good recovery').

flashcards.front: Test that shows the total deviation

flashcards.back: The covered eye moves inwards to recover.
1 cm at 1 m = 1Δ; or neutralise with a prism bar (base in for exo, base out for eso).

flashcards.front: Which cover test reveals intermittent tropias?

mcq.q: You cover the right eye and the left eye moves inwards to take up fixation. What does this show?

options.feedback: Yes — the left eye was turned out and moved in to fixate.
An esotropic eye would move outwards.
Phoria is seen on the covered eye when uncovering.
Movement on cover–uncover means a tropia.

mcq.explanation: On cover–uncover, a movement of the uncovered eye means it wasn't fixating — a tropia. Inward movement means it was out (exo).

mcq.q: What target do you use for a distance cover test in a patient with 6/9 in the worse eye?

options.text: A letter one line larger than 6/9

options.feedback: Only if VA is worse than about 6/18.

options.text: The biggest letter on the chart

mcq.explanation: The target should be one the worse eye can just see clearly, so a letter one line larger than its best acuity is used.

mcq.q: Cover the left eye; the right eye moves in to fixate. What is it?

options.feedback: Tropias show on covering the other eye.

mcq.explanation: Covering the left eye forces the right to fixate. It moved in, so it was turned out: a right exotropia.

mcq.q: How long do you watch after covering?
mcq.explanation: Watching for 2–3 seconds gives the uncovered eye time to take up fixation, without letting the patient lose interest.

mcq.q: The prism bar for exo deviations is placed
mcq.explanation: Prism is placed with the apex towards the direction of the deviation, so an exo deviation is neutralised with base-in prism.

mcq.q: What does 1Δ correspond to?
mcq.explanation: One prism dioptre displaces a ray 1 cm at a distance of 1 m.

mcq.q: Smooth, fast recovery on uncovering suggests
mcq.explanation: Smooth, quick recovery on uncovering shows fusion easily controls the phoria, so it's compensated.

mcq.q: When should near cover test be done looking down?
mcq.explanation: If there are near symptoms, testing in downgaze, the usual reading position, can reveal a deviation missed in primary gaze.

mcq.q: Which statement about the cover test is wrong?

options.text: It can't tell a phoria from a tropia
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: it's the only objective test that can.

options.text: It's done at distance and near

mcq.explanation: The cover test is the only objective test that distinguishes phoria from tropia.

original.q: Why is the cover test unique?

options.text: It's the only objective test that distinguishes phoria from tropia

mcq.q: Which test reveals the total deviation (phoria plus tropia)?
mcq.explanation: The alternating cover test breaks fusion completely, so it shows the total deviation (phoria plus any tropia).

mcq.q: Covering the fixing eye shows movement of the other eye. What is it?
mcq.explanation: If the other eye moves when the fixing eye is covered, it wasn't pointing at the target: a tropia.

mcq.q: With an exotropia, covering the fixing eye makes the deviated eye move
mcq.explanation: In exotropia the deviated eye points outwards, so it moves in to take up fixation.

mcq.q: A right hypertropia: covering the left eye makes the right eye move
mcq.explanation: In a right hypertropia the right eye is higher, so it moves down to take up fixation when the left eye is covered.

mcq.q: Why might a tropia show no movement on cover?

options.text: Eccentric fixation or a tiny microtropia
It's always visible, so this can't happen
The occluder used is too large
The patient has closed their eyes

mcq.explanation: With eccentric fixation, or a microtropia too small to see, the eye may not visibly move.

mcq.q: How do you measure a deviation with prisms?

options.text: Add prism until the movement stops
Measure the movement with a ruler
Read it off with a focimeter

mcq.explanation: Prism is increased until there's no movement on alternate cover; that prism equals the deviation.

mcq.q: Why use an accommodative target at near?

options.text: A spotlight works just as well

mcq.explanation: An accommodative target controls accommodation, which affects convergence and so the size of the deviation.

mcq.q: How long should each eye be covered?
mcq.explanation: About 2–3 seconds is long enough for the eye to drift but not so long that fixation is lost.

mcq.q: What does recovery speed tell you?
mcq.explanation: Slow or jerky recovery suggests fusion is struggling to control the phoria.

mcq.q: When is the cover test done?

options.text: At distance and near, with and without Rx

mcq.explanation: Deviations can differ with distance and with the prescription, so the cover test is done at distance and near, with and without Rx.

mcq.q: The simultaneous prism cover test measures
mcq.explanation: The simultaneous prism cover test measures only the manifest deviation (the tropia), with fusion otherwise kept.

mcq.q: An eye that drifts up when covered, with no matching hypotropia of the other eye, suggests
mcq.explanation: In DVD, each eye drifts up when covered, without the matching movement a true hypertropia would show.

mcq.q: Nystagmus that appears only when one eye is covered is
mcq.explanation: Latent nystagmus appears or increases when one eye is covered.

mcq.q: A wide nasal bridge or epicanthic folds can create
mcq.explanation: Epicanthic folds or a wide nasal bridge hide the nasal sclera, so straight eyes can look esotropic.

mcq.q: A positive angle kappa can make the eyes look
mcq.explanation: A positive angle kappa displaces the corneal reflex nasally, which can make straight eyes look exotropic.

mcq.q: The Hirschberg test uses

options.text: a red glass and a light

mcq.explanation: The Hirschberg test estimates a deviation from the position of the corneal light reflexes.

mcq.q: The Krimsky test measures a deviation by

options.text: using prism to centre the reflexes

mcq.explanation: The Krimsky test places prism in front of an eye until the corneal reflexes are centred, measuring the deviation.

mcq.q: An esotropia that's straight with full hyperopic glasses is
mcq.explanation: If the eyes are straight when the full hyperopic correction is worn, the esotropia is fully accommodative.

mcq.q: Infantile esotropia typically begins
mcq.explanation: Infantile esotropia usually starts before 6 months of age and is large-angle.

mcq.q: An alternating tropia means

options.text: either eye can fix, with the other deviating
the deviation comes and goes over time
the right eye is always the one that turns

mcq.explanation: In an alternating tropia, either eye can take up fixation while the other deviates.

mcq.q: A microtropia is usually

options.text: a phoria rather than a tropia

mcq.explanation: A microtropia is small, usually under about 10Δ, and is often associated with amblyopia.

mcq.q: Why test at distance and near?

options.text: It's simply how it has always been done
They're always the same, so it's a check
To fog accommodation between the tests

mcq.explanation: Deviations can be quite different at distance and near, so both must be tested.

mcq.q: Why repeat the cover test with and without the Rx?

options.text: To save time in the routine
So the practice can bill it

mcq.explanation: Glasses change accommodation and therefore convergence, which can change the deviation.

mcq.q: Which is the correct order of cover tests?
mcq.explanation: The cover-uncover test is done first, because the alternate cover test breaks fusion and could make a phoria look like a tropia.

mcq.q: After the alternate cover test, why watch the eyes when you stop?

options.text: To see how fast fusion recovers
It isn't needed at the end

mcq.explanation: Watching as you stop shows how quickly the eyes regain fusion, a sign of how well the phoria is compensated.

mcq.q: A slow, jerky recovery suggests
mcq.explanation: Slow, jerky recovery means fusion is struggling, so the phoria is poorly compensated.

mcq.q: Which target is used at distance?

options.text: A letter a line above the worse VA

mcq.explanation: A letter one line above the worse eye's acuity keeps both eyes fixating and controls accommodation.

mcq.q: Esodeviations in prism cover testing are neutralised with
mcq.explanation: Esodeviations are neutralised with base-out prism.

mcq.q: An exotropia of 20Δ means the eye is turned out by about
mcq.explanation: One prism dioptre is about 0.57°, so 20Δ is about 11°.

mcq.q: Which abbreviation means exophoria in many UK records?
mcq.explanation: In many UK records, XOP means exophoria.

mcq.q: Which abbreviation means esotropia?
mcq.explanation: SOT (or ET) means esotropia; XOT is exotropia, XOP exophoria and SOP esophoria.

mcq.q: Why is a cover test important in children?

options.text: It finds strabismus that causes amblyopia
It measures the child's eye pressure
It checks the child's colour vision

mcq.explanation: The cover test detects strabismus, which can cause amblyopia if not found and treated early.

mcq.q: A child's eye turns in only at near when reading. What should you check?
mcq.explanation: An eye turning in only at near suggests an accommodative cause, so check for hyperopia and a high AC/A ratio.

mcq.q: Which is a sign of a constant unilateral tropia?

options.text: The same eye always turns, often amblyopic
Fixation switches between the two eyes
No movement is seen on cover-uncover

mcq.explanation: In a constant unilateral tropia the same eye always deviates, and it's often amblyopic.

mcq.q: In an intermittent tropia, the patient may
mcq.explanation: When the eyes are straight in an intermittent tropia, fusion is present and stereopsis can be good.

mcq.q: Why do you watch the uncovered eye when covering?

options.text: To check the acuity of that eye
It isn't needed for the test

mcq.explanation: If the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation, it wasn't pointing at the target, revealing a tropia.

mcq.q: Why should the patient keep looking at the target during the test?

options.text: So that they remember to blink

mcq.explanation: If the patient looks away from the target, the eyes move for that reason, giving false results.

mcq.q: Which near cover test position suits a presbyope who reads looking down?

options.text: In downgaze, with their reading Rx

mcq.explanation: A presbyope reads in downgaze through their reading Rx, so test there to see their real binocular state.

mcq.q: A tropia found in an adult with new double vision should prompt

options.text: a search for a cause, e.g. a palsy

mcq.explanation: A new tropia with diplopia in an adult may come from a nerve palsy or other disease, so the cause must be found.

mcq.q: Which eye movement is seen when uncovering an esophoric eye?
mcq.explanation: An esophoric eye drifts inwards behind the cover, so on uncovering it moves outwards.

cases.scenario: BVP SAQ: in primary gaze the right eye is turned in.
cases.question: Name the deviation [1] and describe the distance cover/uncover test findings [4].
cases.modelAnswer: Right esotropia [1]. Cover LE: RE moves out to take up fixation, and LE moves in under the cover (Hering's law) [1]. Uncover LE: RE moves back in to its deviated position and LE moves back out [1]. Cover RE: neither eye moves [1]. Uncover RE: neither eye moves [1].

topics.askClaude: Describe what you see during cover tests (which eye moves, which way, on cover or uncover) and ask me to name the deviation each time.

topics.title: Fixation disparity and the Mallett unit
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: within Panum's fusional area the eyes can be slightly misaligned and still see singly. This fixation disparity is likely with a decompensated phoria, and the Mallett unit measures the aligning prism that removes it.
keyPoints: Panum's fusional area: each retinal point corresponds to an area on the other retina; single vision is kept over a small space in front of and behind the horopter (Panum's fusional space).
Fixation disparity: a small misalignment within Panum's area; exo, eso, hyper or hypo slip.
Aligning prism (once called associated phoria): the prism that removes the fixation disparity.
Near Mallett set-up: polaroid visor over the near Rx, text matching their near VA, check both nonius strips are seen.

Ask if the strips line up with the X; if not, find the smallest base-in prism (exo slip) or base-out prism (eso slip) that aligns them. Repeat with the vertical OXO and vertical prism, and ask about tilt (cyclodeviation).
At near, extra plus can remove an eso slip by reducing accommodative convergence.
examTraps: Asking leading questions ('Is the line moving to the left?').
Confusing the aligning prism with the dissociated phoria from the cover test.

diagram.description: Mallett OXO target: letters O X O in the centre (seen by both eyes), a polarised vertical line above (seen by one eye) and below (seen by the other). Left panel: lines aligned with the X. Right panel: lower line shifted sideways — a horizontal slip.

goDeeper.heading: When are prisms indicated?
goDeeper.body: The answer sheet notes that good prism adaptation argues against prescribing prism for a slip with asthenopia. Consider the slip together with symptoms and other compensation tests.

flashcards.back: A small vergence error within Panum's area that still allows single vision.
The prism that eliminates the Mallett slip (associated phoria).
OXO — seen by both eyes to lock fusion.

mcq.q: A patient has a 10Δ exophoria on the cover test but no Mallett slip and no symptoms. Interpretation?

options.feedback: Yes — no slip and no symptoms.
Dissociated phoria size alone doesn't decide.
The cover test showed a phoria.

options.text: The Mallett unit must be faulty

mcq.explanation: Compensation depends on how well fusion copes, not the dissociated size. No slip, no symptoms → compensated.

options.text: The near Mallett nonius strips may align if plus lenses are added for a patient with a near eso slip
options.feedback: Yes: less accommodation means less convergence.

options.text: The OXO targets are the only part of the Mallett unit seen monocularly
options.feedback: The OXO is seen binocularly (fusion lock); the nonius strips are seen one by each eye.

options.text: Prism correction is indicated for retinal slip with asthenopia and good prism adaptation
options.feedback: Good prism adaptation argues against prisms.

mcq.explanation: Less accommodation means less convergence.

mcq.q: In the Mallett unit, the OXO is seen by
mcq.explanation: The OXO is seen by both eyes and acts as a fusion lock, keeping the eyes fused during the test.

mcq.q: On the near Mallett unit, the strips show an eso slip that 2Δ removes. Which prism base removes it?
mcq.explanation: An eso slip is neutralised with base-out prism (or extra plus at near).

options.text: Stress on vergence, often a decompensated phoria
Normal binocular vision and nothing more
Amblyopia of the eye with the slip

options.text: The misalignment is within Panum's area
They have a small constant tropia
The Mallett unit is out of adjustment

options.text: The smallest prism that removes the slip
Any prism that stops the slip

mcq.q: Which question avoids leading the patient?

options.text: 'Are the lines in line with the X?'

options.text: The vertical OXO and any tilt

mcq.explanation: After the horizontal test, check the vertical OXO for vertical slips and look for any tilt.

options.text: Polarised strips around a fused OXO
Red and green filters over each eye
Full occlusion of one eye at a time
A vertical prism in front of one eye

mcq.explanation: Polarised strips are seen by one eye each, while the central OXO is seen by both, keeping the eyes fused.

mcq.explanation: Mallett is 'associated' because it measures with the eyes still fused, unlike dissociated tests such as the cover test.

mcq.q: An exo slip is neutralised with

options.text: base-out prism in front of one eye
plus lenses added to the near Rx
vertical prism split between the eyes

mcq.explanation: An exo slip means the eyes tend to diverge; base-in prism or minus lenses (adding accommodative convergence) correct it.

mcq.q: Which unit checks foveal suppression?
mcq.explanation: The Mallett polarised letters are seen by one eye each, so missing letters on one side shows foveal suppression.

mcq.q: Is there a distance Mallett unit?
mcq.explanation: There is also a distance Mallett unit, used at about 6 m.

mcq.explanation: A slip with symptoms suggests a decompensated phoria.

mcq.explanation: A little minus stimulates accommodation and the convergence that goes with it, which can reduce an exo slip in a young patient.

mcq.q: Why is the aligning prism often a good guide for prescribing prism?

options.text: It's measured with the eyes still fused
It equals the full dissociated phoria
It measures the reading add needed
It isn't used to guide prescribing

mcq.explanation: The aligning prism is measured with the eyes fused, as in everyday viewing, so it reflects what will relieve symptoms.

mcq.q: Why ask 'Are the lines in line with the X?' rather than 'Is the line moving?'
mcq.explanation: Asking about movement suggests an answer; asking whether the lines are in line with the X avoids leading the patient.

options.text: No: check for a vertical slip too

mcq.explanation: After the horizontal test, check the vertical strips.

original.q: Which slip is checked after the horizontal one?

mcq.q: Under which lighting is the Mallett unit used?
mcq.explanation: The Mallett unit is used in normal room lighting, which reflects everyday viewing.

mcq.q: At what distance is the near Mallett unit used?

options.text: One metre and no other distance

mcq.explanation: The near Mallett unit is used at the patient's reading distance, often 40 cm.

mcq.q: What does the OXO provide?
mcq.explanation: The OXO is seen by both eyes and provides a central fusion lock.

mcq.q: An associated phoria is measured
mcq.explanation: An associated phoria is measured while the eyes stay fused.

mcq.q: A patient sees only one of the nonius strips. What does it suggest?
mcq.explanation: Each nonius strip is seen by one eye, so seeing only one shows the other eye is suppressing.

mcq.q: How is a Mallett result recorded?

options.text: e.g. 'N Mallett: no slip H and V'

mcq.explanation: Results are recorded specifically, for example 'N Mallett: no slip H and V' or the aligning prism needed.

mcq.q: An eso slip in a young hyperope may be helped by

options.text: minus lenses over the near Rx
nothing: eso slips can't be helped

mcq.explanation: Plus lenses relax accommodation and the convergence that goes with it, and base-out prism also corrects an eso slip.

mcq.q: Why test the Mallett unit with a presbyope's near add?

options.text: Results depend on the lenses worn

mcq.explanation: The lenses change accommodation and convergence, so the result depends on what's worn; test through the near add used.

mcq.q: Which device can plot fixation disparity against prism?
mcq.explanation: A disparometer plots fixation disparity against prism, giving a forced vergence curve.

mcq.q: Which card is a near fixation disparity test?
mcq.explanation: The Wesson card is a near test of fixation disparity.

mcq.q: A slip that appears only after a few seconds suggests
mcq.explanation: A slip that appears after a few seconds suggests the phoria is only just being held and is starting to decompensate.

mcq.q: Why might a large dissociated phoria have no Mallett slip?

options.text: The phoria is really a tropia
It's impossible: there'd be a slip

mcq.explanation: Good fusional reserves can control a large phoria, so there may be no slip and no symptoms.

mcq.q: An aligning prism usually compares with the dissociated phoria as
mcq.explanation: The aligning prism is usually much smaller than the dissociated phoria, because fusion is still working.

mcq.q: Which slip direction is an exo slip?

options.text: The strips shift as if the eyes turned out
The strips move upwards and downwards
The strips stay lined up with the X
One of the strips disappears entirely

mcq.explanation: An exo slip looks as if the eyes have turned out, which shows as a crossed displacement of the strips.

mcq.q: When should you increase prism to find the aligning prism?
mcq.explanation: Prism is increased only until the slip just disappears, giving the smallest aligning prism.

mcq.q: Which part of the Mallett unit tests vertical slips?

options.feedback: Yes: rotate or use the vertical test.

mcq.explanation: Rotating the unit (or using the vertical test) uses horizontal strips, so the vertical alignment can be checked.

mcq.q: Mallett results help decide whether to
mcq.explanation: Mallett results help decide whether to prescribe prism, change the lenses or give exercises.

mcq.q: What should you ask if the patient sees the strips moving?

options.text: Where do they settle against the X?
Does the line look red to you?

mcq.explanation: Strips may move, so ask where they settle against the X; the settled position gives the slip.

mcq.q: The distance Mallett unit is used at
mcq.explanation: The distance Mallett unit is used at about 6 m.

mcq.q: Polarised filters in the Mallett unit

options.text: let each eye see its own strip

mcq.explanation: Polarised filters let each eye see only its own strip, so a slip between the eyes can be seen.

mcq.q: Which group is the Mallett aligning prism threshold often stricter for?

options.feedback: Yes, different guidance for under and over 40.

mcq.explanation: Guidance on how much aligning prism matters differs by age, and the threshold is often stricter for younger patients.

mcq.q: The foveal suppression test letters get
mcq.explanation: The foveal suppression letters get smaller down the scale, like an acuity chart.

mcq.q: A patient suppresses the smallest letters with one eye. What does it suggest?
mcq.explanation: Missing the smallest letters with one eye only suggests foveal suppression in that eye.

mcq.q: Why is Mallett preferred for prescribing prism over dissociated tests?

options.text: It measures prism with the eyes fused
It isn't preferred: cover test is

mcq.explanation: Mallett measures the prism needed with the eyes fused, as they normally are, so it's a better guide than dissociated tests.

mcq.q: Which vertical aligning prism is usually clinically significant?
mcq.explanation: Vertical fusional reserves are small, so even 1Δ of vertical aligning prism can matter if the patient has symptoms.

mcq.q: What's a key limitation of fixation disparity tests?

options.text: Results vary with time and light
They need drops to be instilled

mcq.explanation: Fixation disparity results can vary with time of day, fatigue and lighting, so they aren't perfectly repeatable.

mcq.q: Which test should follow a Mallett slip?

options.text: Nothing more: the slip is enough

mcq.explanation: A slip should be followed up with fusional reserves and the patient's symptoms, to decide on management.

mcq.q: Which near Mallett finding needs no action?
mcq.explanation: With no slip and no symptoms, binocular function is coping well and nothing needs doing.

mcq.q: Spheres rather than prism are preferred when

options.text: they correct the slip and suit the refraction

mcq.explanation: Spherical lenses are preferred when they remove the slip and also suit the patient's refraction, avoiding prism.

mcq.q: Which is the dissociated equivalent of the Mallett test?
mcq.explanation: Dissociated tests such as the cover test and Maddox wing break fusion, unlike Mallett.

cases.question: Describe how you'd use the near Mallett unit to investigate fixation disparity and measure aligning prism.
cases.modelAnswer: Set-up (up to 2): polaroid visor over the near Rx; ask them to read text matching their near VA; check both green nonius strips are seen. Then: ask if the strips line up with the X; if not, find the smallest base-in (exo slip) or base-out (eso slip) prism that aligns them [2]; repeat with the vertical OXO using vertical prism [1]; ask whether the strips look tilted (cyclodeviation) [1].

topics.title: Convergence insufficiency
topics.summary: Convergence insufficiency (CI) is a common cause of near-work symptoms: the eyes struggle to converge and hold convergence. Typical signs are a receded near point of convergence, more exophoria at near than distance, and reduced positive fusional reserves at near.
keyPoints: Symptoms with near work: eyestrain, headaches, blur, double vision, words moving, losing place, poor concentration.
Receded near point of convergence (NPC) — clinics often use a break of about 6–10 cm or more as abnormal (check your criteria).
Exophoria greater at near than at distance.
Reduced base-out (positive) fusional reserves at near, often failing Sheard's criterion.
Rule out other causes: uncorrected refractive error, accommodative insufficiency, convergence paresis (neurological).

Treatment: vergence/accommodative therapy — office-based therapy with home reinforcement had the best results in the CITT trials; home exercises (e.g. pencil push-ups, dot card, stereograms) are common first steps.
Base-in prism for near can help some adults but is less effective in children.
examTraps: Measuring NPC with a non-accommodative target.
Forgetting to measure recovery as well as break.
Missing an underlying refractive or accommodative problem.

diagram.description: Side view: an RAF rule with a target moving towards the patient's nose. Both eyes converge until one eye drifts out (break point). The break distance in cm is marked; recovery shown as the target is moved back until both eyes refixate.

goDeeper.heading: Measuring NPC
goDeeper.body: Use a small accommodative target (e.g. a line of print on an RAF rule) at about 40 cm, move it slowly towards the nose and ask the patient to say when it goes double — and watch the eyes. Note the break and the recovery as you move it away. Repeat a few times: a near point that recedes with repetition suggests poor stamina.

goDeeper.heading: Exercises
goDeeper.body: Dot card: a card with dots along a line; patient converges on each dot, keeping it single with the others seen double. Pencil push-ups: follow a target in towards the nose until it doubles, then back. Stereograms and jump convergence build fusional reserves. Keep them short, regular and progress gradually; review after a few weeks.

flashcards.back: Receded NPC, exo greater at near, reduced positive fusional reserves at near.
Office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement.

mcq.q: A 15-year-old has headaches reading, NPC break 14 cm, 2Δ exo at distance and 12Δ exo at near, low base-out reserves. Most likely?

options.feedback: Basic exo is similar at distance and near.

mcq.explanation: Exo greater at near, receded NPC and reduced convergent reserves = CI.

mcq.q: Which is typical of convergence insufficiency?

options.text: Exophoria greater at near than distance

mcq.explanation: Convergence insufficiency typically shows an exophoria that's larger at near than at distance.

mcq.q: Which symptom is common in CI?

options.text: Words moving or losing their place
Blur at distance and nothing else
Flashes of light in one eye

mcq.explanation: In CI, convergence is hard to keep up at near, so words seem to move or the reader loses their place.

mcq.q: A 14-year-old's NPC break is 12 cm, recovering at 16 cm. How do you interpret it?

options.text: It can't be judged from this

mcq.explanation: A break of about 6–10 cm or more is often considered abnormal.

original.q: What NPC is often considered abnormal?

options.text: A break of about 6–10 cm or more

options.feedback: Very abnormal, but the threshold is lower.

mcq.q: Parents ask which convergence insufficiency treatment has the best evidence. What do you say?

options.text: Pencil push-ups at home on their own
Placebo exercises with a reward chart
Patching the dominant eye each day

mcq.explanation: In CITT, office-based vergence therapy with home reinforcement had the best results.

original.q: Which treatment had the best results in the CITT trial?

options.text: Office-based vergence therapy with home reinforcement

mcq.q: In a patient with convergence insufficiency, which near fusional reserve do you expect to be low?
mcq.explanation: CI shows reduced positive (base-out) fusional reserves at near.

original.q: Which fusional reserve is reduced in CI?

mcq.explanation: Rule out uncorrected refractive error, accommodative insufficiency and convergence paresis.

original.q: Which must be ruled out?

options.text: Uncorrected refractive error, accommodative insufficiency and convergence paresis

mcq.q: Base-in prism for near helps
mcq.explanation: Base-in prism for near can help some adults with CI, but trials showed it isn't effective in children.

mcq.explanation: CI often fails Sheard's criterion, because the base-out reserve is less than twice the near exophoria.

mcq.q: Which test helps assess convergence quickly?
mcq.explanation: The near point of convergence and jump convergence are quick tests of convergence.

mcq.q: In CI, which fusional vergence is reduced?
mcq.explanation: In CI, positive (base-out) fusional vergence is reduced, so the patient can't converge comfortably at near.

mcq.q: Which questionnaire measures CI symptoms?
mcq.explanation: The Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey (CISS) measures CI symptoms.

mcq.q: Which exercise helps CI?
mcq.explanation: Dot cards and the Brock string train convergence and awareness of fusion.

mcq.q: In CI, the exo is
mcq.explanation: In CI, the exophoria is larger at near than at distance.

mcq.q: The AC/A in CI is typically
mcq.explanation: CI is typically associated with a low AC/A ratio, so accommodation produces little convergence.

mcq.q: A patient with CI also has a low amplitude for age. What does this suggest?
mcq.explanation: Accommodative insufficiency often coexists with CI.

original.q: Which may coexist with CI?

mcq.q: Office-based vergence therapy versus pencil push-ups in CITT?
mcq.explanation: The CITT trial found office-based vergence therapy with home reinforcement worked best for symptomatic CI.

mcq.q: What is 'jump convergence'?

options.text: Switching fixation far to near fast
A sport used in vision therapy
A prism used to train vergence
A type of cover test at near

mcq.explanation: Jump convergence means switching fixation quickly between a far and a near target.

mcq.q: NPC is recorded as
mcq.explanation: The NPC is recorded as the break point (diplopia) and the recovery point.

mcq.q: Which near phoria fits CI?

options.text: More exo at near than at distance

mcq.explanation: CI shows more exophoria at near than at distance.

mcq.q: Which home exercise uses beads on a string to show physiological diplopia?
mcq.explanation: The Brock string uses beads on a string to show physiological diplopia and train convergence.

mcq.q: When fixating a Brock string bead correctly, the patient sees

options.text: the strings crossing at that bead

mcq.explanation: When fixating a bead correctly, the two strings appear to cross at that bead.

mcq.q: Eccentric circle (lifesaver) cards train
mcq.explanation: Eccentric circle (lifesaver) cards train fusional vergence without instruments.

mcq.q: Typical vergence therapy courses last about
mcq.explanation: Vergence therapy courses usually last about 12 weeks.

mcq.q: Which group can develop CI after an injury?
mcq.explanation: Convergence insufficiency is common after concussion.

mcq.q: Which neurological disease is associated with CI?
mcq.explanation: Convergence insufficiency is associated with Parkinson's disease.

mcq.q: Which finding points to convergence paresis rather than convergence insufficiency?

options.text: A sudden onset with other neurological signs
Gradual near symptoms in a student

mcq.explanation: Distinguish CI from convergence paresis (neurological) and accommodative insufficiency.

mcq.explanation: In children, a CISS score of about 16 or more suggests symptomatic CI.

mcq.q: Vergence facility is often tested with

options.text: 12Δ base out and 3Δ base in flippers
±2.00 D lens flippers held at near
a pinhole occluder over each eye
a Maddox rod and a spotlight

mcq.explanation: Vergence facility is often tested by flipping 12Δ base-out and 3Δ base-in prisms.

mcq.q: A red glass in front of one eye during NPC testing helps
mcq.explanation: A red glass in front of one eye makes it obvious when the image doubles, showing the break point.

mcq.q: Positive fusional vergence is measured with
mcq.explanation: Positive fusional vergence is convergence, measured with base-out prism.

mcq.q: Which result supports CI?
mcq.explanation: Low base-out reserves at near support a diagnosis of CI.

mcq.q: Why combine office and home therapy?

options.text: Office guides technique; home adds practice
Home therapy alone is always enough
There's no real reason to combine them

mcq.explanation: Office sessions guide correct technique, and home exercises add practice between visits.

mcq.q: Base-in prism reading glasses for CI

options.text: may help some, on weaker evidence

mcq.explanation: Base-in prism reading glasses may help some patients, but the evidence is weaker than for vergence therapy.

mcq.q: Why check accommodation in CI?
mcq.explanation: CI and accommodative problems often coexist, so both should be checked.

mcq.q: Plus lenses for near can help CI when

options.text: the AC/A is low and accommodation is normal

mcq.explanation: Plus lenses help when there's also accommodative insufficiency, though they can worsen the exo.

mcq.q: Which symptom suggests CI rather than presbyopia in a 15-year-old?
mcq.explanation: Diplopia or words moving at near suggest CI; a 15-year-old is too young for presbyopia.

mcq.q: What should you do if CI symptoms persist after therapy?
mcq.explanation: If symptoms persist, reassess the diagnosis and consider orthoptic referral.

mcq.q: Which test is used in CITT to define a receded NPC?
mcq.explanation: In the CITT, a receded NPC was defined as a break of 6 cm or more.

mcq.q: Jump vergence improves
mcq.explanation: Jump vergence training improves how quickly the eyes can converge.

mcq.q: Which is a computer-based vergence therapy?
mcq.explanation: Computer programs such as HTS provide vergence therapy at home.

mcq.q: A low AC/A ratio means

options.text: little convergence per dioptre of accommodation
a lot of convergence for each dioptre
no accommodation at all at near
the patient is likely to be myopic

mcq.explanation: A low AC/A ratio means accommodation produces little convergence.

mcq.q: Why record recovery of the NPC as well as break?

options.text: So the clinic can bill for it
It's always the same as break

mcq.explanation: Poor recovery of the NPC, as well as a receded break point, suggests CI.

mcq.q: Why measure the near phoria in CI?

options.text: CI shows more exo at near

mcq.explanation: CI shows more exophoria at near, so measuring the near phoria helps confirm it.

mcq.q: What's 'pseudo-CI'?
mcq.explanation: Pseudo-CI is poor convergence caused by weak accommodation, which drives less accommodative convergence.

mcq.q: A patient with CI and reading complaints should also be checked for
mcq.explanation: An uncorrected refractive error can cause similar symptoms, so an accurate refraction is essential.

mcq.q: Pencil push-ups alone are
mcq.explanation: In the CITT, pencil push-ups alone were less effective than office-based therapy.

mcq.q: CI is most commonly diagnosed in

options.text: the very elderly, and no one else
nobody: it's an extremely rare finding

mcq.explanation: CI is most often diagnosed in school-age children and young adults, as near work increases.

mcq.q: Why is follow-up important after CI therapy?
mcq.explanation: CI symptoms can return after therapy, so follow-up is important.

mcq.q: Stereograms used in therapy train
mcq.explanation: Stereograms train fusion and control of vergence.

cases.scenario: A 20-year-old student gets headaches and occasional double vision after about twenty minutes of reading. Near point of convergence is 15 cm, with a moderate exophoria at near and none at distance.
cases.question: What is the likely diagnosis and how would you manage it?
cases.modelAnswer: Convergence insufficiency: a remote near point of convergence, exophoria greater at near, and usually reduced positive fusional reserves at near, with symptoms on sustained near work. Correct any significant refractive error first, then give convergence exercises such as pencil push-ups, jump convergence and dot card or stereogram exercises, with a review in a few weeks. Base-in prism for near is an option if exercises fail. Refer if it is of sudden onset, associated with neurological signs, or does not respond.

topics.title: Prism prescribing basics
topics.summary: Prism moves the image so the eyes don't have to work as hard to fuse. Use it for symptomatic decompensated phorias (and some tropias) when other options aren't enough — usually the smallest amount that relieves symptoms, split between the eyes.
keyPoints: A prism dioptre (Δ) displaces light 1 cm at 1 m.
Images are displaced towards the apex; the eye turns towards the apex.
Exo deviation → base-in prism; eso → base-out; right hyper → base down right (or base up left).
Split horizontal prism equally between the eyes; vertical prism is usually split too (base down one eye, base up the other).
Base on Mallett aligning prism or Sheard/Percival calculations, then trial it in a trial frame.
Prism can be ground in or produced by decentration (Prentice: c (cm) = P ÷ F) if the lens power allows.
Fresnel press-on prisms are useful for trials or temporary needs (but reduce VA and contrast).
examTraps: Prescribing the full dissociated phoria as prism.
Forgetting to check the prism can actually be achieved by decentration with the lens power and blank size.

diagram.description: Two eyes looking through prisms. Exophoria example: base-in prisms in front of each eye (bases towards the nose), with the images displaced outward towards the apices so the eyes don't need to converge as much.

goDeeper.heading: Notation
goDeeper.body: Write prism with power and base direction for each eye, e.g. R 1Δ BI, L 1Δ BI (total 2Δ BI). For vertical: R 1Δ BD, L 1Δ BU (total 2Δ right hyper relieved). Some clinics use 360° base notation; follow your department's format.

goDeeper.heading: Decentration instead of ground prism
goDeeper.body: Prentice: P = cF, so c (cm) = P ÷ F. For 1Δ base in with a −4.00 D lens, c = 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 cm = 2.5 mm. Direction: a minus lens is thickest at its edge (base away from the OC), so to put base in front of the eye you move the OC outwards (temporally). A plus lens is thickest at its centre (base towards the OC), so for base in you move the OC inwards (nasally). Sketch it to check, and make sure the blank size allows the decentration.

flashcards.front: Which way does the image move through a prism?

flashcards.back: Base down right (or base up left), usually split.

mcq.q: How much decentration gives 2Δ with a +5.00 D lens?

options.feedback: That's for 2Δ with an 8 D lens.
c comes out in cm: 0.4 cm = 4 mm.

mcq.explanation: Prentice's rule rearranged: c (cm) = P ÷ F.

No prism — vertical prism is never prescribed

mcq.q: A prism displaces the image towards its

1Δ base up R and 1Δ base down L

original.q: A right hyper deviation is corrected with

options.text: base down right (or base up left)

mcq.q: A patient needs 4Δ base in. How is it usually prescribed?

options.text: 4Δ base in in the right eye only

mcq.explanation: Horizontal prism is usually split equally between the eyes.

original.q: How is horizontal prism usually prescribed?

mcq.q: What decentration gives 2Δ from a −4.00 D lens?
mcq.explanation: Prentice's rule: decentration (cm) = prism ÷ power = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 cm.

mcq.q: A patient has new diplopia from a sixth nerve palsy that may recover. Which prism suits best?
mcq.explanation: Fresnel prisms suit trials and temporary needs, though they reduce VA and contrast.

original.q: What are Fresnel prisms useful for?

options.feedback: Yes, though they reduce VA and contrast.

mcq.q: Which approach to prescribing prism is best?

options.text: Measure it, then trial it in a trial frame

mcq.explanation: Base prism on the Mallett aligning prism or Sheard/Percival, then trial it.

original.q: How should prism be decided?

options.text: From Mallett aligning prism or Sheard/Percival, then trialled
From the cover test alone always

mcq.q: The eye turns towards the
mcq.explanation: The image moves towards the apex, so the eye turns towards the apex to look at it.

mcq.q: You need 1.5Δ base in from a −5.00 D lens. How?

options.feedback: Yes: minus lenses decentre away from the base.

mcq.explanation: Decentration = 1.5 ÷ 5 = 0.3 cm = 3 mm. A minus lens is thickest at the edge, so to get base in you decentre outwards.

mcq.q: 2Δ base in plus 2Δ base up gives a resultant of about
mcq.explanation: Perpendicular prisms combine like vectors: √(2² + 2²) = √8 ≈ 2.8Δ.

mcq.q: Prism for esophoria is
mcq.explanation: Base-out prism displaces the image inwards, towards where the esophoric eye points.

mcq.q: A patient needs 3Δ base down R. Which split is equivalent?

options.text: 1.5Δ base down R and 1.5Δ base up L
1.5Δ base down R and 1.5Δ base down L

mcq.explanation: Base down in one eye is equivalent to base up in the other.

original.q: Vertical prism of 2Δ base down R can be split as

options.text: 1Δ base down R and 1Δ base up L

mcq.q: Why split prism between eyes?
mcq.explanation: Splitting prism between the eyes keeps the two lenses a similar thickness and weight, which looks and feels better.

mcq.q: A Fresnel prism's drawback is
mcq.explanation: Fresnel prisms are thin but reduce acuity and contrast because of their ridges.

mcq.q: Why is horizontal prism usually split equally between the eyes?

options.text: For equal thickness, weight and appearance
Because one eye can't take prism

mcq.explanation: Splitting horizontal prism equally balances the lenses.

original.q: How is horizontal prism usually split?

mcq.q: Why might a patient need more prism over time?
mcq.explanation: The vergence system can adapt to prism, so the patient may later need more to stay comfortable.

mcq.q: Which test guides vertical prism prescribing?
mcq.explanation: The vertical aligning prism on the Mallett unit is a good guide to how much vertical prism to prescribe.

mcq.q: What happens to prism if a patient's eyes look away from the OC?
mcq.explanation: Looking away from the optical centre induces extra prism (Prentice's rule), which adds to or subtracts from the prescribed prism.

mcq.q: R 3Δ base in and L 2Δ base in give a total of
mcq.explanation: Horizontal prism in the same direction adds between the eyes: 3Δ + 2Δ = 5Δ base in.

mcq.q: R 2Δ base up with L 1Δ base down gives

options.feedback: That needs base down on the right.

options.text: 1Δ vertical, as the two cancel out
No vertical effect, as they cancel

mcq.explanation: Base up on the right and base down on the left both have the same vertical effect, so they add to 3Δ, correcting a left hyper.

mcq.q: 6Δ base in and 8Δ base up combine to
mcq.explanation: Perpendicular prisms combine like vectors: √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10Δ.

mcq.q: How much decentration gives 1Δ from a +2.50 D lens?
mcq.explanation: Decentration = prism ÷ power = 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4 cm, which is 4 mm.

mcq.q: You need 2Δ base out from a −8.00 D lens. How?

options.feedback: Yes: minus lenses decentre opposite the base.

mcq.explanation: Decentration = 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 cm = 2.5 mm. A minus lens gives base out when decentred inwards.

mcq.q: Prescribed 4Δ base out is usually split as
mcq.explanation: Prescribed prism is usually split equally, so 4Δ base out becomes 2Δ base out in each eye.

mcq.q: What limits how much prism you can get by decentration?

options.text: The blank size and lens power

mcq.explanation: Decentration is limited by the size of the lens blank and the lens power: low powers need large decentrations.

mcq.q: Yoked prisms are
mcq.explanation: Yoked prisms have their bases in the same direction in both eyes, shifting both images the same way.

mcq.q: Yoked prisms may be used to

options.text: shift gaze or ease a head posture

mcq.explanation: Yoked prisms shift the field of gaze, which can help with an abnormal head posture or a field defect.

mcq.q: Base-out prisms in both eyes can help some nystagmus by
mcq.explanation: Base-out prism makes the eyes converge, which can damp some types of nystagmus.

mcq.q: Peli prisms are used for
mcq.explanation: Peli prisms expand the field of awareness in homonymous hemianopia.

mcq.q: Fresnel prisms usually reduce VA by about
mcq.explanation: Fresnel prisms usually reduce acuity by about a line, more with higher powers.

mcq.q: Why use a temporary Fresnel prism for an acquired palsy?

options.text: It's cheaper in the long run

mcq.explanation: Deviations from acquired palsies often change or recover, so a temporary, cheap Fresnel prism is ideal.

mcq.q: A prism's base is the
mcq.explanation: The base of a prism is its thickest edge.

mcq.q: Light passing through a prism bends towards the
mcq.explanation: Light passing through a prism bends towards the base.

mcq.q: For an exotropia, the eye turns out, so the image needs moving
mcq.explanation: Base-in prism displaces the image outwards, towards the apex, matching the outward-turned eye.

mcq.q: For an esotropia, which prism helps?
mcq.explanation: Base-out prism displaces the image inwards, matching the inward-turned eye.

mcq.q: Why prescribe the minimum prism that relieves symptoms?

options.text: Mainly to save the patient money

mcq.explanation: The minimum prism avoids adaptation, which can lead to needing ever more prism, and keeps lenses thinner.

mcq.q: Why check prism with the patient after dispensing?

options.text: So the practice can bill for it

mcq.explanation: Checking after dispensing confirms that the prism actually relieves the patient's symptoms.

mcq.q: Prism dioptre and degree are related by
mcq.explanation: One prism dioptre is about 0.57°.

mcq.q: A 2Δ base-down prism over the right eye has the same vertical effect as

options.text: 2Δ base up over the left eye

mcq.explanation: Base down on the right moves the right image up, which has the same relative vertical effect as base up on the left.

mcq.q: Prism thinning in progressives is

options.text: not a prescription: equal both eyes

mcq.explanation: Prism thinning is equal base-down prism in both eyes to make progressives thinner, so it has no binocular effect.

mcq.q: When is prism often avoided in children?

options.text: When exercises or glasses can fix it

mcq.explanation: In children, exercises or the right glasses often fix the problem, so prism is avoided where possible.

mcq.q: Ground prism is preferred over decentration when

options.text: a lot is needed or the blank's too small
the lens itself has no power

mcq.explanation: Ground prism is needed when a lot of prism is required, or the blank is too small for the decentration.

mcq.q: Base-in prism for near can help
mcq.explanation: Base-in prism for near can help some people with convergence insufficiency.

mcq.q: Which test can confirm a vertical prism prescription?

options.text: A trial frame trial with the Mallett unit

mcq.explanation: Trying the prism in a trial frame with the Mallett unit confirms it removes the vertical slip.

mcq.q: A patient adapts to prism and symptoms return. What's the risk of increasing it repeatedly?

options.text: It tends to cause myopia over time

mcq.explanation: Each increase can be adapted to, so repeatedly adding prism risks ever-increasing amounts.

mcq.q: Looking through a base-in prism held before the right eye, where does a straight-ahead object appear?

options.feedback: Light bends that way; the image moves the other way.

mcq.explanation: A prism shifts the image towards its apex.

original.q: A prism shifts the image of an object

mcq.q: A 5Δ prism displaces an image at 1 m by
mcq.explanation: One prism dioptre displaces an image 1 cm at 1 m, so 5Δ displaces it 5 cm.

mcq.q: Prescribed prism on a spectacle Rx is written with

options.text: amount and base for each eye

mcq.explanation: A prism prescription must give the amount and base direction for each eye.

cases.scenario: A symptomatic patient has a decompensated exophoria at near. On the Mallett unit, 2Δ base in is the least prism that aligns the nonius strips.
cases.question: What prism do you prescribe, how is it split, and what is the downside of relieving prism?
cases.modelAnswer: Prescribe the minimum prism that eliminates the fixation disparity, here 2Δ base in for near, usually split as 1Δ base in each eye to balance thickness and weight. Base in relieves an exo deviation and base out an eso deviation. The downsides are that some patients adapt to the prism so the deviation appears to grow, it treats the symptom rather than the fusional weakness, and it adds thickness and cost. Exercises are often tried first for exophoria at near, with prism kept for those who don't respond.
